data.title: China’s Electric Aviation Advantage Is A Transport System, Not A Prototype
data.description:
The electric-aviation contest is often presented as a race between aircraft startups. That is probably the wrong unit of analysis. An airplane that flies once, wins a certification milestone or accumulates a large order book has demonstrated something useful, but it has not demonstrated an industry. What matters is whether operators can put hundreds of aircraft into regular passenger and cargo service, maintain them, charge them, replace their batteries economically, order a second fleet after seeing the real operating costs and eventually sell the system abroad.

China is unusually well positioned for that test because it is not approaching electric aviation as an isolated aircraft problem. Its transport system is already removing many of the routes that aircraft serve poorly. China’s high-speed rail network reached about 50,400 kilometres by the end of 2025 and is expected to approach 60,000 kilometres by 2030. Dense city pairs can remain rail markets, leaving thinner regional routes, islands, difficult terrain, cargo links and poorly connected cities as a more clearly defined aviation opportunity.

That is an important inversion. Seen from an aircraft manufacturer’s sales department, every successful high-speed rail line removes potential passengers. Seen from a transport ministry, rail and aviation have different jobs. China does not need battery aircraft to compete with 350 km/h trains between dense major cities. It needs them to become the better transport product on routes where another railway has poor economics and conventional regional aviation remains too expensive or infrequent.

The full analysis in TFIE Strategy Briefing goes deeper into the battery systems, COMAC and AECC programs, CAAC’s operating framework, the Western countercase and the export pathways that could turn early domestic fleets into an industry.

The threshold for “scale” should be correspondingly demanding. A fleet of electric trainers is not the same thing as a regional passenger market. A few subsidized demonstration routes do not prove utilization or maintenance economics. The stronger evidence would be hundreds of runway-based electric or hybrid aircraft flying repeated schedules, batteries reaching expected replacement intervals, operators understanding real maintenance costs, second orders arriving and foreign operators doing the same.

China already has a small but real certified electric-aircraft base, but that is not the central advantage. Europe certified the Pipistrel Velis Electro in 2020, so China is hardly alone in getting electric aircraft through certification. The more important difference is industrial context. The IEA says China produced more than 80% of global battery cells in 2025, along with even larger shares of some key active materials. Aviation batteries have much tougher mass, safety, power and lifecycle requirements than automotive packs, but electric aircraft developers in China can specialize an industrial base built for markets orders of magnitude larger than aviation.

CATL makes the distinction clear. The company has publicized an aviation-oriented condensed cell at up to 500 Wh/kg, an eye-catching number that becomes much less useful if treated as an installed aircraft-system specification. Real aircraft batteries also require containment, thermal management, electrical protection, battery management, structure, reserves and enough power late in a flight. CATL’s more recent aviation work includes certification-oriented safety testing on a lower-specific-energy configuration, evidence that the company is working both the energy-density and integration sides rather than merely publishing a laboratory number.

Policy matters because aircraft alone do not create scheduled transport. China’s Green Aviation Manufacturing Development Outline for 2023–2035 explicitly includes electric propulsion, aviation batteries and the systems needed to integrate them into civil aircraft. CAAC’s short-haul aviation operating framework deals with the boring but essential pieces—routes, schedules, airport integration, passenger service and operating oversight. That matters more to a real transport market than another spectacular prototype flight because airports need power, airlines need reliable charging windows, crews and maintenance organizations need training, and regulators need experience with battery and propulsion failure modes.

China’s state aerospace industry is also participating rather than leaving the field entirely to venture-backed startups. COMAC-associated programs are doing electric-propulsion and aircraft integration work, while AECC describes a megawatt-class hybrid propulsion system intended for applications extending into next-generation regional aircraft. None of that establishes a certified 70- or 90-seat hybrid airliner today. It establishes that the difficult bridge from small battery aircraft toward larger regional systems is already inside the work programs of organizations responsible for China’s wider aerospace capability.

The Western countercase is strong enough that this remains a forecast rather than a foregone conclusion. Heart Aerospace’s X1 demonstrator flew for 27 minutes in August 2026, at more than 25,000 pounds takeoff weight with over one megawatt of electric propulsion. Europe has certified electric propulsion hardware, established airframers and serious testing environments. Airbus, ATR, Embraer, Safran, Pratt & Whitney Canada, Collins and others have deep aerospace experience China is still building.

China’s advantage is that it can connect those pieces into a deployment system faster. Its batteries come from an enormous manufacturing base, its regulator has explicit institutional reasons to build expertise, its state aerospace organizations can remain involved through multiple development cycles, and its transport system already separates dense rail corridors from routes where smaller aircraft can add more value.

Exports would be the stronger test. China does not need FAA or EASA validation before an electric aircraft can become commercially relevant outside China. COMAC has already demonstrated the broader precedent: by early 2026, C909 aircraft were operating commercially in Southeast Asia, supported through certification acceptance, leasing, training, maintenance and operating support. Electric aircraft are more dependent on batteries and charging infrastructure, but the commercial principle is similar. The export product is not just an airframe; it is the aircraft, ground power, battery support, spares, maintenance, training, finance and regulatory acceptance together.

That is why the next prototype flight is not the most interesting milestone. Watch for delivered aircraft entering repeated service, utilization accumulating, battery replacement intervals becoming visible, operators placing second orders and foreign fleets following domestic ones. Those events would show that China had crossed the line from electric-aircraft development into an electric-aviation industry.

China has not crossed that line yet. It has, however, assembled more of the surrounding industrial and transport system than any other country currently pursuing it. If hundreds of useful aircraft enter routine service, second orders follow and exports begin accumulating operating history, the argument will have moved from industrial forecast to demonstrated leadership.

Read the full systems analysis in TFIE Strategy Briefing.

data.title: An EV Is Not The Same As A Conventional Car. Who Knew?
data.description:
Electric, shmetric. A car is a car, right? You get in, start it up, and go where you need to go. What’s the big deal? That sort of thinking is what nearly killed Hertz after its owners — a couple of B School whiz kids with more money than brains — decided to buy 100,000 Teslas and rent them out like they were Kia Souls and Toyota Corollas. Oops! They forgot to tell their customers about how and where to charge them.

Their idiocy nearly put the company back into bankruptcy.

The truth is, an EV is different than a conventional car, and yet automakers and dealers do a miserable job of informing their customers about those differences. This summer, my wife and I met someone driving a Volkswagen ID.4. Her three year lease was nearly up, and she was leaning toward getting a conventional car instead. Her primary concern was that her condo association refused to allow her to install an EV charger. When we told her our Chevy Bolt was plugged into a standard wall outlet about 90 percent of the time, she was shocked! No one ever told her she could charge her car using just a wall outlet.

Living in New Hampshire where it gets chilly in the winter, she was also disappointed by how long it took to charge her car when the temperatures outside dropped below freezing. When we told her about preconditioning the battery in cold weather, her eyes glazed over. Three years with an EV and the word “preconditioning” had never been mentioned to her. Shame on Volkswagen for letting a customer out the door without a proper orientation, and double brickbats to the dealer who allowed that to happen.

There are a few areas that distinguish an EV from a conventional car, and, since no one wants to talk about them, we feel it is our duty to take up the slack. The two primary areas that need to be addressed are range and charging.

Let’s get to it, shall we?

Range

A conventional car wastes an incredible amount of the energy contained in a gallon of gasoline. A typical new car or truck today only converts 20 percent or less of that energy into forward motion. The rest is mostly wasted as heat. Let’s put this into perspective. An EV with a 65 kWh battery has about the same energy potential as two gallons of gasoline. Maybe in the future, batteries will exist that have an energy density similar to gasoline, but, for the time being, such batteries are just a gleam in some physicist’s eye.

That difference means we need to think differently about electric cars.

The first thing anyone asks about an EV is, “What is its range?”  The EPA calculates range based on information provided by manufacturers, but how accurate are its predictions? Range is basically how far can a car go starting with a 100 percent state of charge until it runs out of battery power and coasts to a stop. But no EV driver in their right mind would do such a foolish thing, would they? Assume you start with 90 percent state of charge and stop to recharge with 10 percent remaining — a much more likely scenario. Now you begin every journey with 20 percent less range. What used to be 300 miles becomes 260 miles.

Then there are all the things that also affect your range — things like speed, hills, temperature, and whether you plan to user the heater or the air conditioner while you drive. Even having the windows open can affect how far you can go, and yet nobody seems to consider those factors. They just want to know the EPA range estimate and assume it will apply to them.

The fact of the matter is that, because conventional cars waste so much energy, driving 85 instead of 70 makes little difference in how far you can go. In an EV, that difference could be 20 percent or more. And while some will see that as a justification for sticking with a conventional car, are you comfortable knowing you are paying almost five bucks a gallon for gas and pissing away 80 percent of the energy you paid for?

Charging

When it does come time to charge your EV, there is whole host of other unknowns to deal with. How do you pay for the electricity you use? Do you need to have a preset amount available with a charging company? How many charging apps do you need? If your car is eligible to use the Tesla Supercharger network, your charging session is billed directly to the credit card you have on file with the company. Otherwise, payment can be an issue.

How do you find an available charger when you need one? Google Maps does a decent job of identifying them in your area. A Better Route Planner and MapQuest do so as well. If you have an account with Tesla, its app will show you detailed information about nearby chargers, including how many there are in total and how many are in use at the moment.

What’s A Charging Curve?

Now let’s consider something most people have never heard of — the charging curve. Lots of manufacturers brag that their cars can charge at 250 kW of power or more, but for how long? The company that makes the car writes the algorithm that controls the charging process. It is designed to keep the battery from overheating and to prolong its service life. That usually means charging speeds begin to taper as soon as the state of charge reaches 40 percent. Above 80 percent, the process may slow down so much that it is actually faster to do two charging sessions from 20 to 70 percent than one from 10 to 100 percent.

Recently, one of our readers reported he routinely has shorter charging sessions than the Tesla vehicles he is sharing a Supercharger location with. That’s because the Tesla algorithm slows down charging much more than the algorithm in his Volkswagen ID. Buzz. Your car’s charging curve will be a major factor in your charging experience, and yet almost no one talks about it — certainly not the manufacturers and dealers who should be educating their customers but refuse to do so. EVKX is an excellent website that supplies accurate information about the charging curves of various EVs. Recurrent is another reliable resource.

Another thing we told the person with the ID.4 was about preconditioning. For fastest charging, the battery needs to be at the proper temperature — not too hot and not too cold. Teslas do this automatically once you select your preferred charging location. For other brands, look in the owner’s manual. It’s in there somewhere, even though you dealer forgot to tell you about it.

The Takeaway

The point is this. An EV is NOT a conventional car, and, if you buy or lease one without understanding the differences, you risk being seriously disappointed. Driving an EV requires thinking differently about your transportation experience. There is a bit more planning needed, for instance. But the reward is a much lower cost of operation, a quieter ride, and the joy of knowing you are not crapping up the atmosphere with the crud that pours out of the tailpipes of conventional cars.

There is also the thrill of instantaneous acceleration and learning to use the precise control regenerative braking makes possible. Some EVs can help you power your home during a blackout. Can your Belchfire 5000 do that?

If you are on the fence about driving an EV, try asking your friends who drive one about their experiences. There are many advantages to electric motoring but also a few quirks that can be unsettling if you don’t know about them in advance. CleanTechnica has many tools available to help educate people about the EV experience. We invite everyone to make use of those resources.

Also, please share your own EV experiences in the comments area below. The more we know, the less anxiety we will have about making the switch to battery power.

data.title: The Day My Swifty Died … And I Had To Go Electric With The MG4…
data.description:
It was the phone call most fathers dread. “Dad, I’ve blown up the car!”

I asked her what had happened to her 20 year old Suzuki Swift (Swifty). “So, the Swift has been making a rattly can noise on and off the whole time I’ve had it. Hubby described it as ‘pinging’, and put it down to dirty injectors or something else lowering the amount of firing. So, on that Thursday, I heard that noise, and needed fuel, but had a bunch of running around to do, so put the increase in the sound of ‘rattling can of stones’ down to getting low to the bottom of the petrol tank and sucking up dirt etc.

“My last trip was to get my son from TAFE, and I knew he would be happy to help me fill the car, and as he’s on his learner’s, also drive home. I told him about the noise, but wasn’t too concerned, as I thought I knew what was going on. About a quarter of the way home, the car started not accelerating much when he pressed the accelerator and he asked me what might be going on. I had no idea, so said to just keep going, we were only 15 minutes from home.

“By this stage, we were on the highway and the car was struggling to reach 100 km/hr. I suggested we just try to limp the car home, as the temp was also increasing to an alarming place on the gauge. We’d just pulled into the ‘slow’ lane on an uphill section of the highway when the car started slowing down and pressing the accelerator wasn’t achieving anything…. We finally came to a stop on a precarious section on the side of the road about 30 meters from a safe place to pull over. We had smoke coming in through all the vents and I honestly thought the car was about to catch fire.

“We hopped out during a break in the traffic and opened the bonnet. Nothing looked out of place, but there was black smoke coming out from behind the engine, so I left it open to try and let it all cool down. When we tried to turn the engine over at this point, it wouldn’t budge (later after it had cooled down, it would turnover, but had zero compression and wouldn’t start).

“A lovely guy in a Suzuki Jimny came and helped my son, Oscar, push us up to the safe spot further up the hill, and waited for my hubby to come and try and sort things out. While he’s not a mechanic, he has rebuilt engines and done considerable work on our classic cars (a 1965 HD GM Holden and a 1966 GM HR Holden). Once he came, he checked the car/engine, decided it was a catastrophic failure, and rang our roadside assistance through our insurance company (Shannon’s, as they are the best for classic cars) and organized a tow truck to tow the Swift home.

“His best guess is that the engine was out of water; it got too hot, so the ring seals were rattling; and we ended up blowing the head gasket and warping the head. Our options were to fix/replace the engine; buy another shitbox; buy a reasonably priced second-hand ICE or EV. [Some of our readers may be quietly thinking — we don’t have any of these issues with electric cars. It was more damage than her mechanic husband and apprentice son could fix. So, it was on the back of a tow truck and off to the heavenly wreckers. The search began.]

One amusing side note: “When Swifty died, I’d just filled her up with petrol. Seventy seven dollars AUS! After emptying the tank, we realized the only thing we had that could use that petrol was our lawnmower, so we’ll be in mower fuel for a while. We bought extra jerry cans and used the petrol pump to empty it. [I suggested she put the petrol on ebay. Their other car is a diesel. Incidentally, it is a Chinese made Tunza with a Cummins engine and BMW running gear based on an older-model Hilux.]

“What I wanted was a second-hand EV, but the market was scarce, I needed to buy a ‘Swift equivalent sized’ new one, as they were around the price I wanted to spend, so I went sitting in cars to see what would ‘fit our family’. We’re all tall and broad shouldered. BYD Atto 1: I didn’t fit, shoulder smooched by B pillar. BYD Dolphin: I mostly fit, again B pillar made hubby not fit on the driver’s side. My hubby’s and my shoulders didn’t fit side by side.

“BYD Atto 2. I fit; hubby mostly fit; again B pillar, and hubby and I fit side by side. But in the back seat there was very little leg room. So, it was up to the next price bracket. Although the Chery sales people were amazingly helpful, knowledgeable and a pleasure to deal with, the seats hurt my kidneys. Otherwise, I would have been happy to buy a car from them. We tried the MG ZS EV, but again, the seats were uncomfortable and the B pillar in the way.

“The sales experience wasn’t so good either: the first second-hand MG ZS EV we looked at I asked the salesman for a state-of-battery health report. He said he had no idea what we were talking about. He did show us the MG4 Urban, and said backseat so big it echoed. He was not wrong!!! And hubby and I both fit in front seat easily. He showed us an older MG 4, but it proved to be too small again. He then showed us the bigger-battery MG4 Urban ex-demo, but got very cagey about the price, battery health, kilometers driven, etc.

“Takeaway: old used car salesman tactics don’t work on EV buyers. We don’t want to buy “new tech to us” car from someone who “doesn’t know” how to sell one. However, we did decide that the MG 4 Urban looked like what we wanted. What we needed was a test drive. Preferably not from the Dodgy Brothers. [Treat yourself to some Aussie humour from the ’80s. Here is clip of the Dodgy brother’s car sales.]

“So we found a better dealership.”

“Jeremy at Hillcrest MG knew ‘everything’ and explained it all in very practical/functional way. He taught us about so much before we even sat in the car, then went through a bunch of things before we drove off. I asked him to do the first part of the test drive so I could concentrate on the screen and the ‘feel’ of the car while he explained everything, before getting behind the wheel myself. I’m so glad I did, because it was such a different driving experience there was no way I could pay attention to the screen while driving or stopping/starting. Amazing driving experience — I was in love and I was buying that ex demo car.

“Side note: We wanted a used vehicle, as I don’t want to contribute further to the consumerism and throwaway economic model that seems so damaging to our country and the world these days. The workaround was getting ex demo. We have bought two brand new cars previously, one ex demo, and multiple used cars both through dealerships and private sales, and also one through a broker.”

[Karryn went on to buy the MG 4 Urban ex demo for $29,990. Sadly, she only received $500 for Swifty. Her purchase is one of the 514 MG 4 Urbans sold in Australia in August — #12 on the Aussie hit parade. I contacted the salesperson, who told me that over 50% of their sales are now electric, and he sees an upward trajectory. He informs me that MG is bringing an electric ute the MG U9 to the Australian market. It can already be ordered and will be showcased at the Everything Electric Show in Sydney at the end of the month.]

“The car works as well around ‘town’ as it does on the highway This is going to sound weird, but there’s also less sensory input. Besides the car having amazing sound deadening, for both road noise and other external noises, because the steering wheel isn’t directly connected to the wheels, I’m not getting constant feedback from the tyres/road, so it’s easier to hold onto. There are only two gears … forwards and backwards … so it is much easier to use and more responsive than even an auto transmission. I don’t have to wait for it to find a gear, or shift down to get power to overtake, take off from slow/stop, etc. Parking with the top-down camera is a breeze, big win there.

Oscar (17 year old): “The Urban is a car made to drive. It’s so much fun because it’s so responsive and easy to drive, an even better ‘go-kart feel’ than the Swift, and that’s even in normal mode (mum won’t let me try sport mode). [That’s] unless we’re on the highway — then it’s boring because the car does just about everything for you.”

“The internal temperature of the car also makes a big difference, so being able to cool the car down using the MG app before I get in definitely helps too. Talking about the app, being able to share the ‘keys’ with anyone is a huge help, as we have three drivers in the family and only two physical keys. Gone are the days we could just ‘have one cut’ apparently — a spare key costs around $700 for a new one! So, two of us have the physical keys, and Oscar will have the key on his phone (once he’s not a learner anymore/gets his provisional license).

“I have only charged at home so far, usually from 8:00am–3:00pm. This gave me 20% (70% up to 90%) purely through solar and/or house battery (when it was shady). I have charging times set at those times in the app, as that’s when our panels put out enough power to supply the house plus whatever we put on top. Oh, and it’s just plugged into a normal wall socket.”

And the last word belongs to Karryn, as her future becomes brighter and more electric: “OMG, the more I drive my car, the more I love it — seriously, so happy with our purchase.”

data.title: EV Chargers in the Tourist Regions of Queensland
data.description:
Tourist regions need high speed charging to drive local economies.

Although there is plenty of access to high-speed charging on the coastal highways and cities of Australia, there is still a need for more charging for tourists once you head inland. This was highlighted by a recent event in Kingaroy, Queensland. Kingaroy is situated at the junction of two highways, D’Aguilar and Bunya Highway. Both are popular tourist drives running through mountains, national parks, and rural townships — and only 218 km northwest of Brisbane. Kingaroy has a population of about 10,000 people.

After driving for a little over two hours, it is a great spot to stop, recharge the car, empty the bladder, and get a coffee. There is one little problem: Tourists with EVs will find it difficult to access high-speed charging. Until recently, there were a couple of level two chargers available, but the high-speed charger was out of order and has been for some time. In winter, many Australians go north from chilly Victoria to soak up the Queensland sun. Kingaroy, with its greenery and boutique wineries, is an attractive spot to stop. It is also the peanut capital of Australia.

The importance of EV charging is recognised by Mayor Kathy Duff. Attended an event organised by Australian Electric Vehicle Association Queensland (AEVA), she said, “EV chargers are a benefit to our region as they encourage more travellers and tourism to the South Burnett.”

When AEVA first started planning the event, the charger had been out of service for several months and the local South Burnett Sustainable Future Network was frustrated that it remained unrepaired. Fortunately, it was repaired before the event and appears to have been operating reliably since.

I asked AEVA members for comment, as I was unable to attend. Allan told me: “I think I only saw about four vehicles charging during the day. Not many attendees appeared to need a recharge, which perhaps says something about either the availability of destination charging or the practical range of modern EVs. We also had a Tesla towing a caravan in attendance, which generated some interest and was a good example of how EVs are increasingly being used for touring and towing applications.

More than 20 electric vehicles attended the Kingaroy event. AEVA members travelled from Mackay, Gympie, the Sunshine Coast, Toowoomba, and Brisbane to participate, along with several local EV owners involved with the South Burnett Sustainable Future Network (SBSFN).

“There was a steady level of public interest throughout the day, with people stopping to chat with EV owners, ask questions, and learn more about electric vehicles and charging. Mayor Kathy Duff was supportive of discussions around EV adoption and future charging infrastructure in the region. Overall, it was a worthwhile event and a good opportunity to raise awareness of EVs in South Burnett.”

“Another point that might be worth mentioning was a conversation with the mayor. She felt that, based on her travel requirements of around 1,200 km per week, often away from home, a hybrid vehicle currently made the most sense for her. It highlighted how important additional fast charging infrastructure is for regional drivers. More charging options across the South Burnett could make EV ownership a much more practical proposition for people with similar travel patterns.”

Don tells me about the different vehicles that were present: “Tesla and Atto 3 were the predominant vehicles. However, [there were] a couple of exceptions — a Mini Cooper EV, an Aion V, a few Hyundais/Kias in various models. I didn’t get the chance to speak with all owners. However, those with whom I did speak were all happy with their vehicles (to be expected really). Although we used the charger twice, we didn’t think to take a photo. The morning just went so quick.”

Kingaroy is a conservative town and I was curious if any FUD was thrown. Robert tells me: “Nothing really it was as you would expect from a conservative area. Although, I was surprised that we had as much interest and as little abuse as we did.” However, there was one notable exception. “There was one [4×4 driver] that had dead gutted pigs hanging off the back of the Ute, sun curing them, and smoking them with carcinogenic diesel soot, yelling abuse out the window as he drove past.” Shame he didn’t have time to get a photo!

Turning to my google research assistant, I am told that there about 80 plug-in electric vehicles garaged within the Kingaroy postcode. “While Queensland as a whole has seen a massive surge in EV adoption, regional areas like the South Burnett have experienced a much slower uptake compared to inner-city Brisbane or the Gold Coast. Regional postcodes across Australia typically average an EV penetration rate of less than 1% of total car registrations.”

While the inner cities battle to find solutions for apartment and kerbside charging, country towns weigh up the decisions around fast charging for the tourists coming through. Who pays for the chargers? Will local businesses gain more from tourists driving electric vehicles than it might cost them to provide charging? I should make it clear — EV drivers should pay for their charging. It appears to be upfront costs that are the big issue.

Perhaps a model with shared costs by business, council, state, and federal governments would work best. But, if we can have high-speed charging at Ayers Rock (Uluru) in the red heart of Australia, surely other tourist destinations can also be equipped.

RACQ makes the point that EV uptake is increasing more rapidly in Queensland’s regions, than in the cities. “Topping the list was the Western Downs region with a 97.8% increase in EV ownership between June 2025 and June 2026, followed by Gladstone with 95.6% and the Somerset region with an 87.2% increase. This compared to Brisbane experiencing a 43.4% lift in EV registrations, the Gold Coast with 47.1% and 60.3% on the Sunshine Coast.”

Executive Manager of Public Policy Dr Michael Kane said “We are seeing decent growth in EVs in western Queensland too.” He highlighted the need for more public chargers to future-proof road tourism in the regions. To many of these towns, tourists are a critical revenue stream. Maintenance issues continue to be a barrier to a thriving EV tourism industry. After all, if a high-speed charger can be installed at Uluru (Ayers Rock) in the heart of Australia, other tourist destinations can also be serviced.

As EV uptake increases throughout rural and regional Australia, thorough planning and strenuous efforts must be maintained to reap the tourist dividend. Not only in the cities, but also in the countryside, the future is bright and electric.

data.title: I Don’t Care What Anyone Says, I Love This Fiat Topolino!
data.description:
It’s no secret here on CleanTechnica, I love smaller cars. I am not a fan of large vehicles. Unfortunately (for me), I’m in the minority on this topic, especially here in the United States. But we still get to see some great, fun, small electric cars. (The 2018 BMW i3 I drive daily is one such example!) Fiat, of course, is one of the brands known for its small vehicles. A famous designer has now gone in and modified a common Fiat model to make it extra cool and fun with two custom designs. Let’s have a look.

Admittedly, the Topolino is not a fully adequate car for the family and road trips on the interstate, it’s not even street legal for use on public roads, it’s not at all a top seller, and it really doesn’t warrant a couple of fancy, custom designs. Nonetheless, these are super cool looking and I guess may attract enough extra buyers to be worth it? Maybe?

How can you not love that?!

In the United States, Fiat has had a shocking drop in sales in recent years. The brand sold 43,772 vehicles in the country back in 2012. That’s not a huge amount, but compare it to what the brand sold in 2025 — 1,321! Fiat has been all but dead in the United States in the past few years, and I expected it to just leave the US market even two or three years ago. But, hey, as long as it’s here, we get fun news like this. The Topolino takes “glorified golf cart” to a new level, but that’s what some buyers want. For $13,995, it’s a lot compared to a used EV with much more capability and range, but that’s perhaps what you would expect for a high-spec, fancy golf cart, right?

Anyway, these specially designed Topolino vehicles were designed by Fabrizio Giugiaro and Lapo Elkann. The models are the Top L and Top J. (L = Love, J = Joy.) The Top L “draws inspiration from the spirit of actor James Dean’s Porsche 550 – dubbed ‘Little Bastard’ – and features a matte aquamarine finish with matching leather upholstery and Alcantara cabin inserts,” Autoblog shares.

“Giugiaro is a car designer and son of Giorgetto Giugiaro, who penned iconic models like the DeLorean DMC-12, BMW M1, and Hyundai Pony – which inspired the Ioniq 5. Meanwhile, Elkann is an Italian entrepreneur and brother of Stellantis Chairman John Elkann.”

Will these designs lead to anything significant? Probably not, but who knows?

data.title: Waymo’s Next Target: Singapore
data.description:
Waymo has expanded its robotaxi service across the United States quite significantly in 2026. It’s not yet covering a huge portion of the population, but it’s operating in more than a dozen major cities already. As it expanded further and further in the US, though, I started wondering how hard it would be for the company to grow into other countries and how much it would try to do so.

Now, however, we’ve got news of it moving into the UK, into Germany, into Japan next year, and the latest news is its next foreign target: Singapore.

The Singapore launched isn’t around the corner. It’s planned for 2028, not next year. However, that also shows us the deliberate, careful approach Waymo takes and its long-term planning. And does anyone doubt Waymo will actually launch service in the unique island city-state in 2028?

Why announce this so early? Well, as just noted, Waymo has a careful and methodical approach to entering new markets, and Waymo vehicles will start arriving in Singapore in coming months to start autonomous vehicle testing, mapping, etc.

Singapore is a highly regulated place, but it’s also a super innovative country that likes to be at the forefront of technology and public policy. In a previous life when I was in the city & regional planning field, Singapore was a hotshot that got a lot of attention for its approach to planning, technology, and transportation. The government will, without a doubt, be very involved in Waymo’s testing and rollout, but it will also be keen to be ahead of the curve in this field.

“Waymo will need approval from Singapore’s Land Transport Authority (LTA) before it can begin accepting passengers. The city-state requires all autonomous vehicles to undergo a safety assessment conducted at the Centre of Excellence for Testing and Research (CETRAN) before they can be deployed on public roads,” The Verge shares. “The tests have been developed by LTA and CETRAN, with input from the Traffic Police. But Waymo isn’t totally unknown in Singapore. The company established a corporate entity there earlier this year and participates in Singapore’s Steering Committee on Autonomous Vehicles.”

Note that we’ve previously covered autonomous bus, autonomous shuttle, other autonomous shuttle, and autonomous streetsweeper progress in Singapore, among plenty of other cleantech matters.

data.title: Discounts on Kia EV9 Give It Ridiculous Price
data.description:
The Kia EV9 is one of the few three-row electric vehicles on the market. It’s quite large, and the interior and technology are very nice and high quality despite the vehicle being fairly affordable. However, apparently, it hasn’t been cheap enough — until some dealerships recently got aggressive with their discounting in order to move more off the lot.

According to Carscoops, a dealership in Texas is providing a $16,041 discount on the EV9 Light RWD, bringing it down from its starting MSRP of $54,900 to a ridiculously competitive $41,414. We’re talking the price of a Tesla Model 3, Tesla Model Y, or Kia Niro EV!

The EV9 Light RWD has only 230 miles of range, but that’s really plenty for the vast majority of buyers. And, yes, we’re talking about a large SUV that can seat up to 7 adults!

I’m personally not a fan of large vehicles, because I don’t like driving them, don’t feel a need for the extra space, and don’t like large vehicles taking up so much space and using so much energy, but this would be a hard deal to pass up or ignore!

There are big discounts on the EV9 elsewhere as well. “At Liberty Auto Plaza in Illinois, an EV Light Short Range has been handed a $15,000 discount, dropping the price from $57,480 to just $42,480,” Autoblog shares. “There’s also a $15k saving on the Light Long Range model, which nets you a more practical 304 miles between charges. This one’s price has been cut from $59,785 to $44,785.” Again, these are ridiculous prices for the large electric SUV. When you consider how much money the EV9 could save you in operational costs compared to a similarly spacious, 7-seat SUV powered by gasoline, the deals are even that much more enticing.

If you’ve been thinking about a Kia EV9 for a while, perhaps now is the time to jump! That is also, apparently, what many buyers have concluded this year so far. Sales of the electric model have been up 12% in the first 8 months of 2026 compared January–August of 2025.

data.title: Driven to Serve: How Taylor Searcy Turned Navy Service into Clean Energy Strategy at GM
data.description:
Most people don’t think about energy until the lights go out. Or transportation until the road is closed. Or the complex systems that keep people moving until they stop working.

Taylor Searcy has spent much of his career thinking about those systems.

Driven to Serve highlights the veterans and military-connected employees who build successful careers at GM with purpose and impact.

As a young Surface Warfare Officer aboard USS Lassen, he stood watch as Officer of the Deck, entrusted with the safe navigation of a $1 billion destroyer and more than 300 sailors. Every hour required situational awareness. Every decision carried consequences. Nothing worked unless the systems — and the people behind them — worked together.

Today, that same sense of responsibility extends beyond the bridge of USS Lassen.

As Clean Energy Strategy Lead at General Motors, Taylor works on the energy GM needs for its assembly plants, high-tech design centers, and offices. That includes helping the company support cleaner energy systems while balancing cost and reliability.

His view of that work grew from experience.

One of his first port visits aboard USS Lassen was to Dili, the capital of Timor-Leste, a Southeast Asian nation north of Australia. There, nightly blackouts showed him how deeply energy affects daily life.

Later, while researching sustainable maritime transportation in Fiji, he saw how remote island communities depended on infrequent visits from unreliable ships for access to goods and services. For many residents, it was their only link to the mainland.

Find out how Taylor connects Navy service, clean energy, and GM’s work today.

What did standing watch teach you about responsibility?

Standing watch taught me that responsibility is not about making every decision alone.

It is knowing what is in your authority, how the team operates, and when something needs to be escalated. As Officer of the Deck, I had to understand the full picture while also knowing when to rely on the chain of command.

That lesson has stayed with me. In any large organization, success depends on bringing the right people into the right decisions.

What Navy experience still helps you in your work today?

One thing I still rely on is building a plan around different courses of action, with contingencies in place from the start. That makes it easier to shift quickly when conditions change.

In the Navy, things moved quickly. Having a plan gave you a roadmap, but it did not mean everything would go exactly the way you expected. You had to think through different scenarios and be ready to adjust.

That still applies today. The work can be complex, so it helps to stay focused on the goal while staying flexible about how to get there.

Was there a moment when you realized how much people depend on reliable energy?

One of the experiences that stayed with me was my first port visit aboard USS Lassen to Dili, the capital of Timor-Leste.

The country had been through a long war for independence, and the electrical grid was still limited. At night, the power would go out regularly. I remember seeing that and realizing how much I had taken reliable, abundant energy for granted.

It wasn’t just about lights. It was about whether daily life could continue the way people needed it to.

I still think about that port visit. It made energy feel like something people depend on, not just something that runs in the background.

What made sustainability and clean energy feel like the right next step after the Navy?

I had been interested in sustainability for a long time, but the Navy made it feel more real.

I had seen places where resources were limited and damaged environments from overexploited resources. I had also seen how much effort it takes to keep ships fueled and operating at sea. That made me think more seriously about the nexus of sustainability and the energy systems people rely on every day.

After active duty, I wanted to do meaningful work that connected those experiences to something positive for people and the planet. That led me to a dual master’s degree program in Japan and Germany, and eventually to a small team in the South Pacific focused on sustainable maritime transportation.

Clean energy made sense to me because it touched the things I kept coming back to: the importance of resilience and interconnectedness of humanity and nature.

How does your work at GM connect energy and transportation?

GM uses a tremendous amount of energy to manufacture vehicles, so reliable and affordable power is essential to our operations.

My work helps GM support cleaner energy systems while managing cost and reliability. I’m really proud that GM secured enough renewable energy to match 100% of our U.S. electricity use in 2025, the first U.S. automaker to reach that milestone.

I also think of electric vehicles as more than a mode of transportation. They are becoming part of the broader energy system. For example, bidirectional charging technology can turn your compatible GM EV into a home backup generator.*

That makes GM’s role in the energy transition especially meaningful to me. Our purpose is to pioneer the innovations that move and connect people to what matters. I have seen what happens when communities lack dependable transportation or energy, so that purpose feels very real to me.

What would you tell other veterans who are looking for their next mission?

Clean energy and sustainability are broad fields. There is room for people with many different backgrounds.

I would tell veterans not to underestimate what they already know how to do. If you have served, you understand responsibility. You understand how to work through uncertainty. You understand what it means to be part of something larger than yourself.

Use your network. Reach out to other veterans. Ask questions. There is no single path into this work.

For me, the connection between the Navy and GM comes back to integrity. At the Naval Academy, I was grounded in the Navy’s core values of honor, courage, and commitment. GM’s behavior of “Win with Integrity” resonates with me because it carries that same idea forward.

The work changes. The mission can too. But the way you carry yourself matters most.

Discover more about how veterans and military-connected employees at GM turn service into impact.

  • Driven to Serve: How Army Reserve Service Guides Jhansi Nalla’s Leadership at GM
  • Driven to Serve: Rain Thompson on navigating life after the Navy
  • Driven to Serve: Brett Munster’s Marine confidence keeps GM moving
  • Driven to Serve: How Alex Reba supports two missions at once
  • Driven to Serve: How John Gillmer champions veterans and data at GM
  • Driven to Serve: Brandon Gifford still owns the mission at GM
  • Shifting Gears: Veterans transition from military service to vehicle service

*Requires a V2H-capable GM EV, GM Energy PowerShift charger and V2H Enablement Kit, a properly equipped home, and proper grid interconnection; performance and duration depend on battery state, weather, and load; not recommended for powering medical devices.

Article by GM.

data.title: BYD Planning 4 Factories in Europe
data.description:
BYD’s big focus at the moment seems to be finding ways to expand globally and grow its sales outside of China as fast as possible. The Chinese market is not the hottest, which is surely part of it, but it’s also clearly a prime time in the transition to electric vehicles and BYD is probably trying to ensure that it captures market share in countries around the world before it’s “too late” — or just much harder to break into a settled market.

Right now, there’s not much competition in most markets across Asia, South America, North America, and Africa. BYD is jumping into a bunch of countries on these continents and gobbling up new customers quickly. There’s already significant competition in Europe, but even in Europe, there are almost no markets where EVs have more than 50% of the market. It’s also a huge market for new-vehicle sales. So, one key target for BYD is the European market.

To help achieve its goals, now that the EU has high tariffs on EVs produced in China, BYD has to set up production facilities in Europe. The news this week is that BYD is planning on having three vehicle assembly plants in Europe and one battery factory there. That’s the plan for now, at least.

“BYD is ​currently starting production at its first ⁠European plant in Hungary and expects ​to decide by the end of the ​year on a second manufacturing site, Alfredo Altavilla told a presentation in Turin on Wednesday,” Reuters writes. “The ​company is looking to acquire and ​refurbish an existing facility rather than build a new ‌plant ⁠from scratch, with Spain and France among its preferred locations, he said.”

That’s currently the long-term plan. Though, naturally, if things go well, that long-term plan could grow; and if things go badly, perhaps BYD will downsize its plans. What do you think — is this plan too big, too small, or just right?

data.title: No Wonder The Tesla Cybercab Launch Was So Underwhelming
data.description:
It was a mystery wrapped in an enigma when Tesla CEO Elon Musk failed to show up for the much-anticipated launch of the company’s new Cybercab in Austin, Texas. Investors also greeted the September 3 event with a less than enthusiastic response, leading Tesla stock to sink throughout the following days. A rebound has occurred since then, but Tesla still has left some questions unanswered — 21 of them, to be exact.

Questions Swirl Around Cybercab Launch, Again

If the September 3 launch was meant to demonstrate Cybercab’s ability to steer itself through the streets of Austin without the benefit of a human operator, maybe it did, and maybe it didn’t. Tesla is pitching the Cybercab as a pure robotaxi, meaning it is designed without a steering wheel or any other sort of human-manipulated controls, though Motortrend is among the auto industry news organizations reporting that the Cybercab can indeed be operated manually, by virtue of a “secret” virtual joystick.

Musk has also been known to show off the forthcoming Optimus “autonomous” humanoid robot with a remote control assist from human operators, so there’s that.

Fully and completely autonomous or not, the September 3 Cybercab launch raised questions about first responder safety, among other concerns. More recently, the Cybercab has attracted a rash of pranksters jumping in front of the robotaxi to “prove” its autonomous driving system works.

Just one day after the Austin launch, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration also jumped in to remind everyone that the Cybercab is not necessarily ready for primetime. “The US Department of Transportation’s National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) today announced that it has opened an Audit Query (AQ) to investigate Tesla’s certification that its new Cybercab meets all applicable Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards (FMVSS),” NHTSA announced.

“NHTSA’s Audit Query will evaluate the technical data and processes Tesla relied upon to self-certify compliance for a vehicle lacking traditional human controls,” NHTSA added for emphasis.

To further cloud the rollout, earlier this week a Cybercab reportedly avoided a routine, 10-minute ride drive and instead chose a 70-minute detour, underscoring the technology’s unreadiness for highway travel.

“Was supposed to be a quick 10 minute hop from 99 Ranch to the Domain. The car had other plans and took me on a massive south detour through East Austin. Guess the Cybercab wanted the scenic route today. Total ride time was 70 minutes,” wrote Reddit poster TyGuy539 on r/Austin.

The Gloves Come Flying Off

Of course, Elon Musk himself oversaw the gutting of staff at NHTSA and other federal offices during his role as the chief of Trump’s budget-hacking “DOGE” office, so it’s unclear how much investigating NHTSA can actually do. Still, the office has some teeth left, and evidently Tesla still has some ‘splaining to do.

As part of the Audit Query, NHTSA issued a  “Special Order” that requires Tesla to submit the technical background supporting its Cybercab self-certification, under oath, by September 30.

“Based on information available to NHTSA, the Cybercab is a purpose-built vehicle that Tesla certified as compliant with all applicable Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards (FMVSS),” NHTSA reminds everyone, especially Tesla Head of Litigation Brian Jazeri and Tesla Associate General Counsel Eric Williams, to whom the Special Order is addressed.

“Self-certification is a foundational responsibility for vehicle manufacturers under the National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act of 1966 (Safety Act), as amended and recodified, 49 U.S.C. Chapter 30,” NHTSA further reminds.

The Special Order lists 21 specific requests for information. In terms of the September 3 demonstration in Austin, #5 is particularly interesting: “Confirm whether the subject vehicles are capable of being driven by a human driver using temporarily attached human driver controls.”

Request #6 is also of interest:

“State whether temporarily installed human driver controls or other equipment for use by a human driver were a part of Tesla’s basis for certifying compliance with any FMVSS. If so, describe the human driver controls and list the FMVSS for which the human driver controls were used as a part of Tesla’s basis for certifying compliance.”

Request #13 further indicates that NHTSA may have caught Tesla in a mistruth regarding the nature of the September 3 rollout.

“State whether the subject vehicles have a turn signal operative unit that is self- canceling by steering wheel rotation. Also state whether the subject vehicles have a manually operated control of a turn signal operating unit,” NHTSA demands, then continues:

“If the answer to any of the previous statements is no, provide in detail how Tesla determined that the subject vehicles complied with FMVSS No. 108 (49 CFR § 571.108) S9.1.1. If your answer differs depending on whether any human driver control or other equipment for use by a human driver is temporarily installed in the vehicle, describe in detail how it differs.”

Tesla Lives To See Another Day

Regardless of the Cybercab kerfluffle, Tesla has maintained its position as the #1 seller of EVs in the US. Other stakeholders were giving the automaker a run for the money until last year, when the premature death of the federal EV tax credit sparked an electrification pullback among Ford and General Motors, among others.

As reported by Kelly Blue Book earlier today, Tesla led other automakers in EV sales for August, with Toyota, Rivian, Hyundai, and Cadillac following up. However, Tesla sales in August were 3.8% lower than in July, while Toyota went up 34.9% in the same period.

More to the point, the overall EV sales picture in the US looks dim indeed, largely if not exclusively due to last year’s sharp U-turn in federal energy policy.

“New EV sales were up 2.5% from July, but down 46.9% from 2025,” KBB notes, referring to the numbers for August. EVs accounted for just 5.7% of new vehicle sales in the US in August, even as the global marketplace jumped to more than 25%.

All else being equal, Trump’s ill-fated war in Iran could help turn the sales slump around. Trump can also take part of the responsibility for enabling Russia to drag out its unprovoked invasion of Ukraine, which is also impacting global oil markets. The conflict was launched by Russian President Vladimir Putin in February of 2022, prompting Ukraine to attack Russia’s oil infrastructure in defense. The attacks have intensified since then, cutting deeply into Russia’s ability to export diesel and gasoline.

With all this in mind, Tesla has an opportunity to see its sales numbers increase over the coming months. Beyond that, it’s anybody’s guess. The new Ford Fathom electric pickup truck is still on track for volume production next year, and Rivian somehow managed to secure a $4.5 billion Energy Department loan to build a new factory in Georgia, among other signs of rising competition in the US market.

Photo: The Tesla Cybercab rollout in Austin, Texas has been colored by many questions, including a list of 21 specific demands for information from the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (courtesy of Tesla via CleanTechnica archive).
